title: Reproducibility vs. Repeatability

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM)

summary: Repeatability is how close results are when the same person repeats the same test, on the same equipment, under the same conditions, in a short timeframe. Reproducibility is how close results are when the test is run under different conditions — a different analyst, instrument, lab, or day.
explanation: Both describe consistency, but at different scopes. High repeatability with poor reproducibility suggests a result is real but sensitive to something that varies between operators, instruments, or labs (calibration drift, technique differences, reagent lot variation). Distinguishing the two matters when troubleshooting an inconsistent result — the fix for a repeatability problem (e.g. operator technique) is different from the fix for a reproducibility problem (e.g. instrument calibration or reagent lot).

comparison.left: Repeatability: nothing — same operator, instrument, conditions, short interval
comparison.right: Reproducibility: at least one condition — different operator, instrument, lab, or time

comparison.left: Whether the method itself is stable under fixed conditions
comparison.right: Whether the method holds up across realistic real-world variation

commonMisconceptions: Using the two terms interchangeably — a method can have excellent repeatability and poor reproducibility, or vice versa.
Assuming a single repeated measurement is sufficient evidence of reproducibility.
